opus-5.5.text:
I think the environment side is actually underrated compared to the model side. People spend a lot of time talking about how smart the model is, but an agent is only as useful as the world it can act in. Over the next two years, I expect a big shift there.

First, the digital world was built for humans. Websites, apps, and enterprise software all assume someone looking at a screen and clicking. So right now agents mostly adapt to human interfaces, using browsers, reading screenshots, and simulating clicks. That works, and it'll keep improving, but it's inefficient. I think we'll see more interfaces designed for agents directly: APIs, protocols, structured tool layers, maybe a kind of "agent-native web." It's a bit like how the internet built mobile-specific versions once smartphones arrived. When agents become a meaningful share of users, products will start serving them as first-class citizens.

Second, infrastructure for running agents will mature: sandboxes, virtual machines, persistent memory, permissions, identity, payment. Today if you want an agent to do a real task over hours or days, you hit practical problems. Where does it run safely? How does it remember context? What is it allowed to touch? Who's accountable if it makes a mistake? These sound like engineering details, but they decide whether agents leave the demo stage and do real work. I'd expect much of the progress over the next two years to come from solving these unglamorous problems.

Third, and this matters to me from a research perspective, environments are also where evaluation and learning happen. A lot of earlier benchmarks were static question-and-answer tests. The more interesting question now is whether an agent can complete a long, messy task in a realistic environment, recover from errors, and deliver real value. So I think we'll see richer environments for training and evaluation, environments with real tools, real ambiguity, and sometimes real humans in the loop. Whoever builds good environments, with good reward signals, will have a big advantage, because that becomes the data and the feedback loop.

And finally, I think the boundary between "the agent" and "the environment" will blur. Today we think of a model plus some tools. But increasingly the useful unit will be the whole system: model, memory, tools, interfaces, and the people it works with. So the question becomes less "how smart is the model" and more "how much useful work can this whole system do in the real world." In two years I'd hope we're asking that question more seriously, with better answers than today.

r001.rationale: The response predicts more agent-oriented interfaces and infrastructure, but does not suggest that the agent ecosystem may remain centralized around super apps.

r002.rationale: It describes agents adapting to existing human interfaces and anticipates agent-designed interfaces, but does not distinguish extending existing environments from creating new environments from scratch.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important shift is that we're moving from a world where the bottleneck was the model to a world where the bottleneck is the environment. For a long time, if you wanted a better agent, you worked on the model: better reasoning, better instruction following, better tool use. But now the models are quite capable, and what's actually limiting them is where they live and what they can touch.

So over the next two years, I expect a few things to happen.

First, environments will become first-class infrastructure. Right now a lot of agent environments are kind of ad hoc: someone wraps a browser, someone wraps a terminal, someone writes a bunch of tool definitions. That works for demos, but it doesn't scale. I think we'll see environments designed from the ground up for agents, with clean state, deterministic resets, good observability, and interfaces that are actually legible to a language model rather than retrofitted from interfaces built for humans. The analogy I like is that early deep learning needed GPUs and frameworks like PyTorch before the research could really take off. Agents need the same kind of foundational layer, and we're still early in building it.

Second, I think the line between environment and training signal will blur. An environment isn't just a place where the agent acts, it's also where the reward comes from. The environments that matter most will be the ones where you can verify outcomes: did the code pass the tests, did the task actually complete, did the user get what they wanted. That verifiability is what lets you do reinforcement learning at scale. So I expect a lot of investment in environments specifically because they generate training data, not just because they're useful products.

Third, there's a hard question about the real world versus simulation. Simulated environments are cheap and safe, but they drift from reality. Real environments, like actual websites, actual codebases, actual company systems, are messy and stateful and sometimes irreversible. I think the next two years will be about building bridges between these: sandboxes that are realistic enough to transfer, and real systems with enough guardrails that an agent can operate in them without causing damage. Permission systems, undo, audit logs, these boring things become really central.

And then honestly, the thing I'm most uncertain about is standardization. Will there be a few dominant protocols for how agents talk to tools and environments, or will it stay fragmented? My instinct is that some standards will emerge because the ecosystem badly wants them, but the standards will be simpler than people expect. The model is flexible enough that it doesn't need a very elaborate interface. It mostly needs a reliable one.

So if I had to summarize: the last few years were about making agents smart. The next two are about giving them somewhere to work. And I think that second problem is actually harder and more interesting than people give it credit for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether tool and environment protocols will standardize, but it does not suggest that the agent ecosystem may remain centralized around super apps.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts ad hoc tools retrofitted from human interfaces with environments designed for agents from the ground up. It does not clearly distinguish extending users’ existing digital environments from creating new environments as two approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see two things happening at the same time. One is that agents will get better at using the digital environments we already have—browsers, terminals, all the software people use. The other is that those environments will start changing to accommodate agents.

Today, a lot of software assumes that a human is sitting in front of a screen, clicking buttons and checking the result. An agent can operate that interface, but it’s often an inefficient way to accomplish the task. Over the next two years, I expect more services to expose interfaces that let agents take actions directly, with clearer descriptions of what an action does and whether it succeeded.

But I don’t think the answer is simply to give everything an API. The harder questions are about permissions and feedback. What can the agent access? Which actions can it take on your behalf? If it makes a mistake, can you understand what happened and undo it? Those are infrastructure problems as much as model problems.

And there’s a kind of chicken-and-egg relationship here. When agents aren’t very capable, there’s little incentive to build environments for them. As they become useful, people invest in that infrastructure, which makes agents more useful again. So I’d expect uneven progress: some workflows become very smooth because the environment supports them, while others remain surprisingly difficult. The model’s intelligence is only one part of the system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existing software and agent-friendly interfaces, but does not suggest the ecosystem may remain centralized around super apps.

r002.rationale: It contrasts agents using current environments with those environments adapting for agents. It does not identify creating new environments from scratch as a second approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see two things happening in parallel. One is that agents will get better at using the digital environments we already have—browsers, terminals, and software interfaces designed for humans. The other is that those environments will start adapting to agents, with more structured interfaces and better ways to expose actions and information.

The interesting question is where those two approaches meet. If an agent needs to click through ten pages to do something, perhaps the software should expose a direct operation. But we can’t expect every website or application to redesign itself, so agents still need to work with existing interfaces.

Over the next two years, I would expect a lot of progress in the infrastructure around execution: giving agents a workspace, managing permissions and credentials, preserving state, and making it possible to inspect what happened and recover from mistakes. A demo can succeed once. A useful system needs to handle failures and continue working reliably.

I also think evaluation will become more connected to these environments. Instead of only asking whether a model gives the right answer, we’ll ask whether it can complete a task, how much intervention it needs, and what it costs. That feedback should help us understand which bottlenecks require better models and which require better infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents using existing interfaces and those interfaces adapting to agents, but does not suggest the ecosystem may remain centralized around super apps.

r002.rationale: It contrasts improving agents’ use of existing environments with adapting those environments for agents; it does not identify creating new environments from scratch as an approach.
